result: High semantic relatedness between initial and later-learned information produces profound proactive facilitation at longer delays, while low relatedness can produce proactive interference. This represents the core finding that semantic relatedness profoundly benefits later-learned memories, with the direction of effect depending on the level of relatedness.
evaluation: All reviewers explicitly affirm this central finding. The editor states the study 'provides compelling evidence that semantic relatedness proactively benefits memory' and 'demonstrates the boundaries of these proactive benefits, showing that when studied items have weaker semantic relationships, proactive interference may be observed.' Reviewer 1 describes this as 'one of the central results' showing 'a stronger semantic relationship between a base pair and an earlier pair has a facilitative effect.' Reviewer 2 notes the study 'compellingly shows that relatedness typically leads to proactive facilitation' with interference 'being thus an exception rather than a rule.' Reviewer 3 confirms 'semantic relatedness overwhelmingly produces PF' except 'in the case of unrelated pairs in a wider stimulus set after a short delay, which produced PI.'

result: Semantic relatedness increases interdependence between initial and later-learned pairs, with this effect being significant in 48-hour delay experiments and present across multiple experimental conditions. Interdependence increases with both cue and target relatedness.
evaluation: Reviewers consistently accept the interdependence findings. Reviewer 2 states 'the study informs our understanding of memory integration, demonstrating how interdependence of memory for related information increases with relatedness.' Reviewer 3 notes the results show 'semantic relatedness overwhelmingly produces...greater memory interdependence between base and supplemental pairs.' The interdependence analyses are described as having 'more converging' results across stimulus sets and metrics compared to memorability analyses.

result: Semantic relatedness accelerates learning of paired associates, with higher cue and target relatedness producing faster base pair learning across experiments. Previously learned supplemental pairs scaffold and hasten learning of base pairs depending on their level of relatedness.
evaluation: Reviewers accept the learning acceleration findings. Reviewer 2 explicitly mentions 'analyses of learning data, demonstrating that relatedness leads to both better final memory and also faster initial learning' as an 'additional strength' of the study. Reviewer 1 notes the finding that 'semantic relationship prompts retrieval of the earlier pair' which facilitates learning. No reviewer questions these learning speed results.

result: In the narrower stimulus set with high overall relatedness, proactive facilitation was observed at 48-hour delay across ΔCue, ΔTarget, and ΔBoth conditions. In the wider stimulus set with lower average relatedness, proactive interference was found in the ΔTarget condition at 5-minute delay, but this effect disappeared or reversed at longer delays.
evaluation: All reviewers accept these condition-specific patterns. The editor notes the study 'demonstrates the boundaries of these proactive benefits' based on relatedness levels. Reviewer 1 states the results show 'when the changed item is very different from the original item there will be interference, and when the changed item is similar to the original item there will be facilitation.' Reviewer 2 describes how 'the direction of the effect can flip across the surface of relatedness values' and praises how 'the whole range of conditions is mapped to convincingly show' these patterns.

result: In the wider stimulus set at 48-hour delay, semantic relatedness between targets and cues showed a continuous relationship with memory outcomes: low relatedness produced proactive interference while high relatedness produced proactive facilitation. Intrusions decreased with increasing relatedness, supporting the remindings account.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 identifies this as a weakness, noting 'in the finer scale results, the continuous relationship between the degree of relatedness and the degree of proactive facilitation/interference is less clear.' The relationship was 'only found in the wider stimulus set' and 'only when GloVe metric for measuring relatedness was used.' The absence of this relationship in the narrow stimulus set 'suggests this could be potentially an all-or-none effect (facilitation for related) rather than a matter of degree.' Reviewer 1 also notes the null result in the narrower set 'isn't clearly informative to the theory,' though acknowledges the positive result is 'consistent with the memory-for-change framework.'

result: In the ΔBoth condition where both cues and targets changed, there were no effects of combined cue+target relatedness on memorability in any experiment, though relatedness did improve interdependence in most experiments. Combined analyses across stimulus sets showed relatedness effects on interdependence but not consistently on memorability.
evaluation: Reviewers accept these ΔBoth condition findings without challenge. Reviewer 3 notes the authors 'performed teasing apart whether cue and target similarity separately influence memorability and interdependence seem to support the rest of their conclusions.' The pattern of interdependence effects being more consistent than memorability effects across conditions is acknowledged by Reviewer 2 as part of the overall findings.

result: Comparing retroactive and proactive designs, retroactive benefits were greater than proactive benefits in conditions showing facilitation, presumably because target responses receive retrieval practice during remindings. A flipped test experiment confirmed this advantage was not due to test order effects.
evaluation: Reviewers accept these between-experiment comparisons. Reviewer 1 notes the work is 'a companion piece to an earlier paper by Antony and colleagues (2022)' and that comparing the two 'is informative.' Reviewer 3 highlights 'the ability to directly compare the current results to their prior results on the retroactive effects of semantic relatedness' as a 'particular strength.' The interpretation about retrieval practice is accepted as the authors provide appropriate caveats about non-random assignment.

result: The results generally support predictions from Osgood's 1949 proposed surface regarding how relatedness affects memory interference and facilitation, though some predictions (such as no PI in the ΔCue condition) were not fully supported.
evaluation: Reviewers consistently praise the connection to Osgood's theory. Reviewer 1 states the work 'fills a gap in the prior literature regarding the cognitive validity of an 80-year-old proposal by Osgood' and notes 'the reader can see where the observed results match Osgood's theory and where they are inconclusive.' The editor describes this as advancing 'our understanding of how memories interact.' Reviewers accept that some aspects don't perfectly match Osgood's predictions but view this as informative rather than problematic.

result: The authors propose that pre-existing semantic relationships increase the likelihood of remindings during new learning, which results in retrieval practice benefits and opportunities to integrate memories. This mechanism explains the differential effects across conditions, with ΔCue showing more consistent facilitation than ΔTarget due to reduced competition.
evaluation: Reviewers accept this theoretical interpretation. Reviewer 1 states 'the results are interpreted in terms of a set of existing theories, most prominently the memory-for-change framework, which proposes a mechanism (recursive reminding) potentially responsible for the facilitative effects.' Reviewer 3 notes the results are 'interpreted in the framework of recursive reminders (Hintzman, 2011)' and that 'interpretations and conclusions were mostly reasonable and included appropriate caveats.' The mechanistic explanation is viewed as consistent with the data patterns.

result: The study employed rigorous methodology with five experiments (N=1000 total), manipulating semantic relatedness (narrower vs. wider stimulus sets), delay (5 min vs. 48 hr), and type of change (ΔCue, ΔTarget, ΔBoth, No Δ, Control), with careful counterbalancing and large sample sizes.
evaluation: All reviewers praise the methodology. The editor highlights 'clean experimental design, rigorous statistics, large N samples, and well-characterized stimuli.' Reviewer 1 calls it 'a potential landmark' for manipulating 'multiple fundamental experimental characteristics using the same general experimental design.' Reviewer 2 emphasizes 'large N sample size, so both significant effects as well as null effects are robust and informative' and calls it 'a highly rigorous body of work that sets a great model for future studies.' Reviewer 3 notes 'the analyses were thorough and well-thought-out.'
